name: GO Classes CS Test Series 2026 | C-Programming | Topic Wise Test 3

question.text:
Which of the following is/are valid assignment(s) of the pointer for the given declaration. An assignment is valid if both pointers are of the same type (pointers are compatible) and get successfully compiled with no warning or error.

int a[4][4];
int *t, **pp;

  1. pp = a;
  2. pp = &a;
  3. pp = *a;
  4. t = a[2];

Consider struct alignment rules as described below –

  1. Each primitive data (int, char, float etc) type requiring $\text{K}$ bytes must be stored at the address must be multiple of $\text{K}.$
  2. Address of structure and structure length must be multiples of $\text{K}_{\max}.$ Where $\text{K}_{\max}$ is the largest size of any primitive element of the struct.

Also, we define internal and external fragmentation of struct as follows–

  • Internal fragmentation is padding used between any two primitive data types of the struct.
  • External fragmentation is padding used at the end of the last element of struct to fulfill $2^{\text{nd}}$ rule requirement of alignment above.

For a given struct below, what will be internal and external fragmentation, respectively? Consider that the system has $8$ bytes of address lines, $4$ bytes of integers, $2$ bytes of short, and $1$ byte of the character.

typedef struct {
    int num_donors;
    char** donor_names;
    char has_soft_seats;
    char location_name[10];
    short height;
} cse_building;
  1. $4, 3$
  2. $5, 2$
  3. $0, 7$
  4. $4, 0$

Consider the given declaration

int arr[3][4];
int (*p)[12];
p = malloc(sizeof(int) * 24); // assume malloc() is successful

sizeof(int) = 4 bytes and sizeof(int *) = 8 bytes.

What will be the output of the following lines of C code ?

printf("%d " , sizeof(arr[2]));
printf("%d ", sizeof(p));
printf("%d", sizeof(*p));
  1. $8\; 8\; 8$
  2. $8\; 8\; 48$
  3. $16\; 8\; 96$
  4. $16\; 8\; 48$

What will be the output of the program below-

int u[] = {1, 7, 8, 3};
int v[] = {-4, 9, 33};
int w[] = {12, 2, 57};

struct t{
    char *c;
    int *t;
}go[] = {"GATE", u, "GOClasses", v, "GATEOVERFLOW", w};

main()
{
    struct t *p = go;
    printf("%s ", ++p -> c);
    printf("%d ", ++*p -> t);
    printf("%d ", *++p[0].t);
    printf("%s ", (++p) -> c);
}
  1. ATE $1\; 9$ GATEOVERFLOW
  2. GATE $-4 \;2$ GATEOVERFLOW
  3. ATE $2\; 7$ GOClasses
  4. None of the above

What will be the output of the following lines of C code?

int a[] = {1,2,3,4};
int *p = (int *)(&a+1);
printf("%d", *(p-1));
  1. $1$
  2. $2$
  3. $3$
  4. $4$

Which of the following may lead to a runtime error for the given declaration of $p?$

int (*p)[5];

  1. p[1][1]

  2. *p[1]

  3. (*p)[1]

  4. p[1]

What will be the output of the following program?

#include<stdio.h>
#include<string.h>

struct _info {
    char **strs;
};
typedef struct _info info;
main(){
    info arr_str[2];
    char *strs1[] = {"GO", "Classes"};
    char *strs2[] = {"GATE", "2023"};
    arr_str[0].strs =strs1;
    arr_str[1].strs =strs2;
    info **da, *a;
    a =arr_str;
    da = &a;
    for (int i = 0; i<2; i++)
        for (int j = 0; j< 2; j++){
            printf("%s ", (((*da)+i)->strs)[j]);
        }
}
  1. GO GATE Classes $2023$
  2. GO Classes GATE $2023$
  3. GATE GO $2023$ Classes
  4. GATE $2023$ GO Classes

Assume that variables $p1, p2$ and $n$ are defined as follows:

int *p1 = (int *) malloc(2 * sizeof(int));
int *p2 = p1 + 1;
int n = 1;


Given $4$ programs and $4$ types of issues below, Check which program is likely to cause which type of issue.

  1. $\text{Prog1-C, Prog2-C, Prog3-A, Prog4-D}$
  2. $\text{Prog1-C, Prog2-D, Prog3-A, Prog4-B}$
  3. $\text{Prog1-C, Prog2-D, Prog3-A, Prog4-D}$
  4. $\text{Prog1-D, Prog2-C, Prog3-A, Prog4-B}$

Consider the following declarations of variables in a system having $4$ bytes for integers.

int a[4][4];
int (*p1)[2];
int (*p2)[2];
int (*t1)[4];
int (*t2)[4];

Suppose array a has base address of $1000$ and initial values of $p1, p2, t1$, and $t2$ are $1040,1064,1044$ and $1076$ respectively.

What will be the value of $p2-p1$ and $t2-t1$ respectively?

  1. $6, 8$
  2. $3, 2$
  3. $12, 8$
  4. $32, 24$

What will be the output of a given program in a little endian system? (Assume int takes 4 bytes)

#include
int main()
{
    char t[] = "abcdefg";
    int *p = t;
    p++;
    char *c = p;
    printf("%c", *c);
}
  1. b
  2. d
  3. e
  4. f

Consider the following C program.

#include<stdio.h>
void fun (int a[5]){
    for (int i =0; i<8; i++)
        a[i] = a[i]+1;
}
main ()
{
    int a[8] = {1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8};
    fun(a);
    for (int i =0; i<8; i++)
    printf("%d", a[i]);
}


Which of the following is/are true about the given program?

  1. Program will exhibit a compiler error since array “a” is of size $5$ in function fun() but for loop in fun() runs till $8.$
  2. Program will exhibit run time error since array “a” is of size $5$ in function fun() but for loop in fun() runs till $8.$
  3. On running the program, the output will be $23456789$
  4. None of the above

What will be the output of the following C code?

#include<stdio.h>
void strXpos(char * dest, char * src) {
    if (src[0] == '\0') {
        dest[0] = '\0';
        return;
    }
    if (src[1] == '\0') {
        dest[0] = src[0];
        dest[1] = src[1];
        return;
    }
    dest[0] = src[1];
    dest[1] = src[0];
    strXpos(dest + 2, src + 2);
}
int main() {
    char s1[10] = "GOGATE";
    char s2[10] = "GO";
    strXpos(s2, s1);
    printf("%s", s2);
}
  1. GOGATE
  2. OGAG
  3. OGAGET
  4. GOAGET

The C code printed below is a version of the C string library call strlen(), which returns the length of a given string.

unsigned int mystrlen(char *c)
{
    unsigned int i =0;
    /* Your code here. */
    return i;
}

Which line of code creates a working and accurate version of strlen()?

  1. while(*c!='\0'){
    i++;
    c++;
  }

  2. while(*c++!='\0') i++;
  3. while(*c++ && i++);
  4. while (c[i++] != '\0');

What is the maximum value of i that will not cause this code to overflow?

It is given that $\textsf{sizeof(int) = 4}$ and $\textsf{sizeof(int *) = 8.}$

int *p = malloc(sizeof(int *) * 2);
p[i] = 2501;

In which of the following case(s) character array must end with null char?

  1. char c[] = "abcd";
  2. char c[] = {'a', 'b', 'c', 'd'};
  3. char c[5] = "abcd";
  4. char c[4] = "abcd";
